title: Requirements management: gather, analyse, justify, baseline
blurb: Establish scope by gathering, analysing, justifying and baselining requirements, so every need traces to a benefit.
question: A city council is replacing its paper parking permits with an online portal. Residents, wardens, IT and finance all have long and sometimes conflicting wish lists. How should the project manager turn these into an agreed scope the project can deliver and control?

teach.h: Requirements are where scope comes from
teach.body: Requirements management is the process of capturing, assessing and justifying stakeholders' wants and needs, then agreeing them as the basis of scope. A typical process runs in four steps: gather, analyse, justify and baseline. In plain English: find out what people need, make sure each need is clear and workable, keep only the needs that earn their place, then agree and fix the list so any later change is controlled.

teach.h: The four steps of requirements management

steps.label: Analyse
steps.sub: Clarify, resolve conflicts, structure, check feasibility

steps.label: Justify
steps.sub: Link each need to a benefit or objective; prioritise

steps.label: Baseline
steps.sub: Agree and freeze the set; control changes from here

teach.caption: The baseline isn't the end: from that point, requirements are managed through change control.

teach.h: Gathering techniques and when to use them
head: Technique
Best for
Watch out for
teach.caption: Most projects use a mix: no single technique captures everything.

teach.body: Unclear or unagreed requirements are a leading cause of project trouble: deliverables get rejected because they aren't what people expected, work is reopened, scope creeps and stakeholders dispute what was agreed. Good requirements management gives a shared, documented understanding of the need, a solid basis for estimates and acceptance criteria, and a baseline against which every change can be judged. Fixing a misunderstood requirement on paper is cheap; fixing it after build is expensive.

teach.h: Analyse: is this requirement good enough?

rows.label: "A permit application completes in under 5 minutes"
"Use the same software as the library"
"Wardens can check a permit by number plate"

teach.note: Analysis also resolves conflicts: the project manager facilitates the stakeholders to reconcile and prioritise, rather than simply picking a side.

teach.h: Justify: trace every requirement to a benefit
teach.caption: Traceability shows why each requirement exists, exposes 'nice to haves' with no business need (gold-plating) and helps assess the impact of later changes.

teach.h: Requirements in linear vs iterative life cycles

rows.label: Baselined
values: High level in Foundations, then per time box

teach.caption: Both life cycles gather, analyse, justify and baseline. They differ in how much is fixed, and when.

teach.text: Exam traps: a baseline is an agreed reference point, not a ban on change; changes after it go through change control. Justifying means linking a requirement to a benefit or objective, not getting it signed off. When two stakeholder groups' requirements conflict, the best first step is to facilitate clarification and reconcile them, not escalate straight away or quietly choose one.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Gather: engage the right stakeholders using suitable techniques (workshops, interviews, observation, prototypes, surveys).
Analyse: make each requirement clear and measurable, resolve conflicts and check feasibility.
Justify: link each requirement to a benefit or objective in the business case, and prioritise.
Baseline: agree and approve the requirements so they become the controlled reference for scope.
Explain the payoff: fewer disputes and rework, less scope creep, and a basis for acceptance and change control.
Requirements management establishes scope: gather, analyse, justify, baseline.
Good requirements are clear, measurable and state the need, not the solution.
Every requirement should trace to a benefit; untraceable ones are challenged.
The baseline is the agreed reference; later changes go through change control.
Linear: detailed baseline early. Iterative: high-level baseline, detail per time box via the backlog.

summary: You can now explain how a project establishes its scope by gathering, analysing, justifying and baselining requirements, and why each step matters. You can also contrast how requirements are fixed in linear projects with how they emerge through a prioritised backlog in iterative ones.

A.q: Which is the correct order of a typical requirements management process?
options: Gather, baseline, analyse, justify
Analyse, gather, baseline, justify
Gather, analyse, justify, baseline
Justify, gather, analyse, baseline
A.why: Requirements are first gathered, then analysed for clarity and feasibility, then justified against benefits, and finally baselined.

whyNot.0: Baselining comes last: you can't freeze requirements before they've been analysed and justified.
whyNot.1: You can't analyse requirements you haven't gathered yet.
whyNot.3: Justifying needs a clear, analysed requirement to link to a benefit, so it can't come first.

A.q: During which step of requirements management are conflicting requirements from two stakeholder groups reconciled?
options: Gather
Analyse
Justify
Baseline
A.why: Analysis clarifies requirements, resolves conflicts and overlaps, structures them and checks they are feasible.

whyNot.0: Gathering collects requirements; conflicts surface here but are resolved in analysis.
whyNot.2: Justifying links each (already clarified) requirement to a benefit.
whyNot.3: Baselining agrees the final set; conflicts should be resolved before this.

A.q: What does it mean to JUSTIFY a requirement?
options: Have the end users sign it off as final
Estimate the hours needed to deliver it
Log it in the change register for review
Link it to the benefit or goal it serves
A.why: Justifying shows why a requirement exists by linking it to a benefit or objective in the business case, which also informs its priority.

whyNot.0: Sign-off happens when the requirements are baselined, not when each one is justified.
whyNot.1: Estimating effort is part of planning, not justification.
whyNot.2: Requirements aren't justified through the change log; that is used after the baseline.

B.q: A user says 'the new system must be fast'. During analysis, what should the business analyst do with this requirement?
options: Make it measurable, e.g. pages load in 2s
Baseline it now and clarify it in testing
Reject it, as speed isn't a valid need
Let the supplier interpret it as it sees fit
B.why: Analysis turns vague requirements into clear, measurable ones, so they can be designed, tested and accepted.

whyNot.1: Baselining a vague requirement stores up disputes at acceptance.
whyNot.2: Speed can be a perfectly valid need; it just has to be made measurable.
whyNot.3: Leaving interpretation to the supplier is how deliverables end up rejected.

B.q: What is the main reason for baselining the requirements?
options: To stop stakeholders ever changing their needs
To give an agreed reference for change control
To prove the team gathered requirements quickly
To replace the business case once it is approved
B.why: The baseline is the agreed, approved set of requirements. It becomes the reference point against which changes are assessed and controlled.

whyNot.0: Change is still possible after a baseline; it is controlled, not banned.
whyNot.2: A baseline is about agreement and control, not speed.
whyNot.3: Requirements support the business case; they don't replace it.

B.q: Warehouse pickers find it hard to describe the workarounds they use with the current stock system. Which technique would reveal their real needs best?
options: Sending an online survey
Interviewing the sponsor
Reading the old contract
Observing them on shift
B.why: Observation shows how work is really done, including workarounds people don't think to mention or can't easily describe.

whyNot.0: A survey relies on people describing their work, which is exactly what they find hard.
whyNot.1: The sponsor is unlikely to know the detail of pickers' day-to-day workarounds.
whyNot.2: The old contract shows what was bought, not how people actually work around it.

C.q: On an iterative app project, a valuable new requirement emerges during the third time box. How is it most likely to be handled?
options: Rejected, as scope was frozen at Foundations
Built at once, as iterative scope is unlimited
Added to the backlog and re-prioritised
Sent to the board, as every change needs one
C.why: In iterative life cycles, new requirements go into the backlog and the product owner prioritises them against the rest, within fixed time and cost.

whyNot.0: Foundations sets a high-level baseline; detail is expected to emerge, so new needs aren't automatically rejected.
whyNot.1: Time and cost are fixed, so new items must be prioritised: something lower may drop out.
whyNot.3: Formal escalation is for changes to the fixed time, cost or overall objectives, not every new backlog item.

C.q: Which is NOT a benefit of tracing each requirement back to a benefit or objective?
options: Showing why each requirement is in scope
Exposing gold-plating with no business need
Helping assess the impact of later changes
Removing the need for acceptance testing
C.why: Traceability doesn't replace acceptance testing: outputs must still be checked against their acceptance criteria.

whyNot.0: Traceability does show why each requirement exists, so this is a genuine benefit.
whyNot.1: Requirements that link to no benefit stand out, which exposes gold-plating: a genuine benefit.
whyNot.2: Knowing what each requirement supports helps judge the knock-on effect of a change: a genuine benefit.

C.q: The sponsor of a parking permit portal asks why several requests from the IT team were removed from the requirements. Which is the best explanation?
options: They couldn't be linked to an agreed benefit
They were raised after the gathering workshop
They came from technical, not business, staff
They would have needed a prototype to test
C.why: During justification, requirements that can't be traced to a benefit or objective are challenged and removed, so the scope only contains needs that earn their place.

whyNot.1: Timing alone isn't a reason to remove a requirement; late needs can still be analysed and justified.
whyNot.2: Technical staff can raise valid requirements; the test is whether they support a benefit.
whyNot.3: Needing a prototype affects how a requirement is explored, not whether it is justified.

reteach.title: Think of planning a wedding
reteach.question: A couple is planning a wedding with input from both families. How do the four steps of requirements management play out?

blocks.h: From everyone's wish list to an agreed plan
blocks.body: First the couple GATHERS ideas: chats with both families, a look round venues, a group message poll. Then they ANALYSE: 'a big party' becomes '120 guests, dancing till midnight', and the clash between a church service and a beach ceremony gets talked through. Next they JUSTIFY each wish against what matters to them: the photo booth stays, the fireworks don't. Finally they BASELINE: the booked plan. A later request for a string quartet is weighed against that plan and the budget.

steps.label: Analyse
steps.sub: Make it specific; settle the clashes

steps.label: Justify
steps.sub: Keep what serves the day you want

steps.label: Baseline
steps.sub: Book it; weigh any later request

blocks.text: Booking the plan (the baseline) doesn't mean nothing can change. It means every change is weighed against what was agreed.

explain.body: Collect requirements from all the relevant stakeholders using a mix of techniques: workshops, interviews, observation, prototypes and surveys. Missing a stakeholder group at this stage is a common reason deliverables are later rejected.

test.q: Users of a new booking screen keep saying they'll 'know what they want when they see it'. Which gathering technique fits best?
options: Running a postal survey
Building a quick prototype
Reading past lessons logs
Holding a sponsor briefing
test.why: A prototype gives users something tangible to react to, drawing out requirements they can't describe in the abstract.

whyNot.0: A survey still asks users to describe needs they can't yet picture.
whyNot.2: Lessons logs help with past mistakes, not these users' needs for this screen.
whyNot.3: A sponsor briefing doesn't involve the users who hold the requirements.

explain.body: Make each requirement clear, unambiguous and measurable; remove duplicates; resolve conflicts between stakeholders; group and structure them; and check they are feasible within the constraints. A requirement should state the need, not prescribe the solution.

test.q: Which activity belongs to the ANALYSE step?
options: Holding workshops to collect needs
Getting formal sign-off of the complete set
Checking each need is clear and feasible
Linking each need to the business case
test.why: Analysis checks requirements are clear, consistent and feasible, and resolves conflicts between them.

whyNot.0: Workshops to collect needs are part of gathering.
whyNot.1: Formal sign-off of the set is baselining.
whyNot.3: Linking needs to the business case is justifying.

explain.body: Link each requirement to the benefit or objective it supports, and use that to prioritise. Requirements that support no benefit are challenged and, if no case can be made, removed. This keeps the scope lean and makes it traceable.

test.q: A requirement cannot be traced to any benefit or objective. What should usually happen to it?
options: It is built first, as it is quick to deliver
It is baselined, then reviewed at handover
It is logged on the risk register as a threat
It is challenged and removed unless justified
test.why: Untraceable requirements add cost and risk without value, so they are challenged and removed unless a genuine benefit is identified.

whyNot.0: Being quick to build doesn't make it worth building; it still adds cost.
whyNot.1: Baselining it would lock unjustified scope into the project.
whyNot.2: It isn't an uncertain event, so the risk register isn't the place for it.

explain.body: Agree and approve the requirements as a fixed reference point. In a linear project this is done in detail in Definition; in an iterative project a high-level baseline is set in Foundations and detail is agreed time box by time box. After baselining, changes are controlled rather than simply absorbed.

rows.label: Baseline
values: High level, then per time box

test.q: Once the requirements are baselined on a linear project, how should a stakeholder's request for a new feature be handled?
options: Through formal change control
Added straight into the baseline
Ignored until the project closes
Approved by end users alone
test.why: After the baseline, any change to the agreed requirements goes through change control so its impact can be assessed and the right authority can decide.

whyNot.1: Adding it directly bypasses impact assessment: uncontrolled scope creep.
whyNot.2: Valid changes shouldn't be ignored; they should be assessed and decided on.
whyNot.3: End users can request changes, but the decision sits with the appropriate authority.
